content: Patient adherence to medication regimens, especially for diseases requiring prolonged treatment like tuberculosis (TB), is often suboptimal, leading to poor treatment outcomes. To address this, material incentives such as cash, vouchers, or food are sometimes provided to reward adherence and remove economic barriers to accessing care. The objective of this study was to evaluate the impact of material incentives and enablers on adherence to diagnostic testing, prophylactic therapy, or curative treatment for TB. A comprehensive search of multiple databases and reference lists was conducted up to June 5, 2015, to identify relevant randomized controlled trials. The quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach, and risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated to compare intervention effects. Twelve eligible trials were identified. Ten were conducted in the United States, targeting specific populations such as adolescents, injection drug or cocaine users, homeless adults, and prisoners. The remaining two trials were conducted in Timor-Leste and South Africa, focusing on general adult populations. Sustained Incentive Programs: Two trials evaluated the impact of material incentives on long-term adherence and treatment completion for active TB. Neither trial demonstrated a clear benefit (RR 1.04, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.14; two trials, 4356 participants; low-quality evidence). In one trial, a daily hot meal as an incentive was poorly received due to the inconvenience of attending the clinic at midday. In the other trial, nurses rationed voucher distribution, prioritizing patients they deemed most deprived. Three trials assessed the effects of material incentives on completing TB prophylaxis, yielding mixed results (low-quality evidence). A significant effect was observed in one trial where drug users received regular cash incentives at each clinic visit in a setting with extremely low treatment completion rates in the control group (treatment completion: 52.8% intervention vs. 3.6% control; RR 14.53, 95% CI 3.64 to 57.98; one trial, 108 participants). However, no effects were seen in a trial involving cash incentives for recently released prisoners (373 participants) or in another trial where parents offered material incentives to teenagers (388 participants). Single, Once-Only Incentives: In specific populations such as recently released prisoners, drug users, and the homeless, material incentives likely improve one-time clinic re-attendance for initiating or continuing anti-TB prophylaxis (RR 1.58, 95% CI 1.27 to 1.96; three trials, 595 participants; moderate-quality evidence). Additionally, these incentives may increase the return rate for reading tuberculin skin test results (RR 2.16, 95% CI 1.41 to 3.29; two trials, 1371 participants; low-quality evidence). Comparison of Different Types of Incentives: Single trials in specific subpopulations suggest that immediate cash incentives may be more effective than delayed incentives provided upon treatment completion (RR 1.11, 95% CI 0.98 to 1.24; one trial, 300 participants; low-quality evidence). Cash incentives also appear to be more effective than non-cash incentives for completing TB prophylaxis (RR 1.26, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.56; one trial, 141 participants; low-quality evidence) and for returning to read skin test results (RR 1.13, 95% CI 1.07 to 1.19; one trial, 652 participants; low-quality evidence). Furthermore, higher cash incentives may be more effective than lower cash incentives (RR 1.08, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.16; one trial, 404 participants; low-quality evidence). Conclusions: Material incentives and enablers may have some short-term benefits in improving clinic attendance, particularly among marginalized populations such as drug users, recently released prisoners, and the homeless. However, there is insufficient evidence to determine whether these interventions can improve long-term adherence to TB treatment.
